questions.question: Why is the compliance window for training-data governance at collection time, not after training?
options: Because regulators do not audit deployed models
Because cookie-consent frameworks ban post-collection use
Because GDPR right-to-erasure does not apply to AI
Once data enters model weights, surgical erasure is not possible; retraining from scratch is the only complete remediation and is prohibitively expensive
questions.explanation: The lesson explains that cookie-consent frameworks were built for reversible tracking, but once data is baked into model weights surgical erasure is impossible -- only full retraining removes it, and that is prohibitively expensive -- so compliance has to happen at collection time, not after training.

questions.question: Roughly how many statutory items does California AB 2013 require developers to publish in a dataset summary?
questions.explanation: The lesson lists California AB 2013's Section 3111(a) as requiring 12 statutory items in the published dataset summary, from dataset sources through whether synthetic data generation is used.

questions.question: Which AB 2013 item is new relative to the Gebru et al. 2018 datasheet structure?
options: Sources or owners of datasets
Whether the system uses or continuously uses synthetic data generation
Cleaning, processing, or other modifications
Time period during which data was collected
questions.explanation: The lesson notes item 12, whether the system uses or continuously uses synthetic data generation, is new relative to the Gebru et al. 2018 datasheet fields, while items like sources, processing, and collection period map onto the older datasheet structure.

questions.question: What is the convergent 2025 DPA principle for LLM training on publicly available first-party content?
options: Training is prohibited under all circumstances
Only synthetic data may be used
Explicit user consent is always required
Legitimate interest can justify training on publicly available first-party content with opt-out and appropriate safeguards; consent is not required
questions.explanation: The lesson traces the Irish DPC, Cologne court, Hamburg DPA, and UK ICO rulings in 2025 to a convergent principle: legitimate interest can justify training on publicly available first-party content given opt-out and appropriate safeguards, without requiring explicit consent.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a partial remediation for the irreversibility problem listed in the lesson?
options: Unlearning (approximate removal measured by MIA)
Influence-function-based localization and selective update
GDPR-mandated automatic weight deletion
Fine-tune-suppression of outputs derived from the data
questions.explanation: The lesson lists unlearning, influence-function-based localization, and fine-tune-suppression as the three partial remediations for the irreversibility problem; it explicitly states there is no practical GDPR right-to-erasure equivalent for trained neural networks, so GDPR-mandated automatic weight deletion is not one of them.

questions.question: What does the Data Provenance Initiative's 'Consent in Crisis' (July 2024) find?
options: Publishers are adding robots.txt restrictions at an accelerating rate; the openly-trainable-upon commons is contracting rapidly, with around 25% of top training sources adding restrictions 2023 to 2024
Synthetic data has fully replaced web data
Consent rates are stable across all sources
Robots.txt restrictions are decreasing year over year
questions.explanation: The lesson cites the Data Provenance Initiative's 'Consent in Crisis' audit finding that publishers are adding robots.txt restrictions at an accelerating rate, with around 25% of top training sources adding some restriction between 2023 and 2024, rapidly contracting the openly-trainable-upon commons.
